job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below is a text-based issue list, not a conclusion that any particular operating strategy would be lawful. **Section 2(1)(B)’s discretionary catchall could defeat several apparent gaps**, and exceptions to this bill would not displace other permitting or environmental laws.

### Definitions and scope

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel rather than aggregate threshold.** The definition measures recovery by “a single vessel,” without aggregating vessels under common ownership, control, or a coordinated project. Multiple vessels could each recover no more than 10,000 metric tons annually without meeting subparagraph (A), although subparagraph (B) could still apply.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Exact threshold excluded.** “More than 10,000” excludes recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year. The provision does not expressly prohibit approaching or reaching that quantity.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual measurement period.** “Per year” could mean a calendar year, a rolling 12-month period, or another reporting year. The choice affects both threshold calculations and when liability begins.

4. **Sections 2(1)(A) and 5—Threshold-crossing and violation days.** The bill does not say whether exceeding the annual threshold makes all earlier recovery that year unlawful, only recovery after crossing the threshold, or something else. That uncertainty directly affects daily civil penalties and fair notice.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—Undefined tonnage methodology.** The text does not specify wet versus dry weight, treatment of sediment and seawater, or whether measurement occurs at collection, lifting, or landing. Different methods could materially change whether the threshold is crossed.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—Depth boundary and measurement.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower falls outside subparagraph (A). The bill also supplies no depth datum or method for evaluating operations spanning different depths, subject again to the catchall.

7. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” is undefined.** It is unclear whether recovery occurs when material is dislodged, collected on the seabed, raised to a vessel, or landed ashore. This complicates classification of equipment testing, partial recovery, and abandoned material.

8. **Section 2(1)(A)—Attribution to a vessel.** The bill does not explain how to attribute recovery involving seabed robots, separate collection and lifting vessels, transshipment, or fixed installations. A system not readily characterized as recovery “by a single vessel” presents a textual gap.

9. **Sections 2(1) and 3(a)—Non-recovery activities.** Exploration, surveying, construction, transport, processing, financing, and purchasing are not expressly included in subparagraph (A). Whether they constitute “engag[ing] in” mining or an activity covered by subparagraph (B) is unresolved.

10. **Section 2(1)—“Commercial” does not require commerce.** Despite the defined term’s label, neither subparagraph requires sale, profit, or a commercial purpose. Large scientific recovery could therefore qualify, while smaller for-profit recovery might not qualify under subparagraph (A).

11. **Section 2(1)(A)—Mineral-resource coverage.** “Other mineral resources” is undefined, leaving questions about mineral-bearing sediment, dissolved minerals, and recovery from subseabed deposits rather than directly “from the seabed.” The bill provides no classification rules.

12. **Section 2(1)(B)—Undefined Secretary.** The bill never identifies “the Secretary” responsible for determining comparable ecosystem risks. Section 6 names the Secretary of State for a different function, but that does not clearly resolve section 2’s assignment.

13. **Section 2(1)(B)—Unspecified risk-comparison standard.** “Risks,” “deep-sea ecosystems,” and “comparable” lack definitions or assessment criteria. The reference activities themselves vary greatly in scale, location, technology, and environmental effects, making the comparator uncertain.

14. **Section 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure or timing.** The bill specifies no process, publication requirement, or effective date for a determination, and does not say whether determinations cover categories or individual projects. This creates notice and enforcement problems, particularly if a determination is applied to earlier conduct.

15. **Section 2(1)(B)—Catchall potentially exceeds the stated subject.** “Any activity” is not expressly limited to mineral recovery, activities below 200 meters, or commercial conduct. Read literally, it could reach unrelated activities with comparable ecosystem risks, creating substantial scope uncertainty.

16. **Section 2(2)—Incomplete coverage of legal entities.** The definition expressly includes citizens and state-organized corporations, but not LLCs, partnerships, trusts, or other noncorporate entities. Their overseas activities may therefore fall outside the “U.S. person anywhere” branch, although conduct in the United States remains covered.

17. **Section 2(2)—Other organizational jurisdictions omitted.** Corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, or foreign law are not expressly included as corporations organized under the laws of “a State.” The bill also provides no ownership-or-control rule covering foreign subsidiaries of U.S. businesses.

18. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Noncitizens abroad.** U.S. residency alone does not make an individual a “U.S. person” under this definition. Noncitizens operating wholly abroad are not expressly covered merely because they reside in, or have business connections to, the United States.

19. **Section 3(a)—Uncertain territorial and participation rules.** The bill does not define “in the United States” or clarify application to territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, U.S.-flagged vessels abroad, or domestic direction of overseas operations. It also does not expressly define indirect participation, leaving the treatment of managers, contractors, and financial supporters uncertain.

### Exceptions

20. **Section 3(b)—Exploration license shields “mining.”** The exception expressly protects mining conducted under an exploration license, without distinguishing exploration-scale recovery from commercial production. Its scope nevertheless depends on what “under” means and what the underlying license actually authorizes.

21. **Section 3(b)—No specified licensing authority.** The exception does not identify the issuing government, agency, or legal regime. Whether foreign-issued or internationally issued exploration licenses qualify is therefore unresolved.

22. **Section 3(b)—No express limits on grandfathered operations.** The text supplies no independent tonnage cap, vessel limit, geographic restriction, or requirement that operations already have begun. Constraints may arise from the license itself, but the exception adds none.

23. **Section 3(b)—Renewals, amendments, and transfers.** The bill does not address whether a pre-enactment license remains qualifying after renewal, expansion, transfer, or changes in operator. Nor does it clearly distinguish permissible changes from a newly issued license.

24. **Sections 3(b) and 8—Grandfathering cutoff differs from effective date.** Licenses issued during the 180-day implementation period are not protected by section 3(b), even though the prohibition has not yet taken effect. Conversely, a license obtained immediately before enactment may qualify without any prior operating history.

25. **Section 3(c)—Undefined environmental-assessment exception.** The exception contains no definition, approval requirement, scale limit, duration limit, or prescribed assessment protocol. Recovery otherwise meeting the mining definition could potentially qualify if genuinely conducted for environmental assessment.

26. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities.** “For the purpose of” does not specify an exclusive, primary, or substantial purpose. The treatment of activities that both assess environmental effects and recover saleable minerals is consequently uncertain.

27. **Sections 3(b)–(c) and 4—Exceptions do not waive reporting.** Both exceptions apply only to section 3(a), not the registry provisions. Exempt mining may therefore remain registrable and reportable, a distinction the bill leaves implicit.

### Registry and enforcement

28. **Section 2(3)—Registry size gap.** A vessel of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less is not a covered vessel, even if it conducts prohibited mining. Vessel size limits reporting coverage, not the section 3 prohibition.

29. **Section 2(3)—Equipment and tonnage uncertainty.** “Equipped for” is undefined, including its application to temporary equipment, support vessels, and equipment removed between deployments. The bill also does not specify the applicable gross-tonnage measurement convention.

30. **Section 4(a)—Unclear jurisdictional reach.** “Each covered vessel” contains no nationality, location, or U.S.-connection limitation. That creates uncertainty over whether NOAA must register foreign vessels operating wholly abroad and how such an obligation could be enforced.

31. **Section 4—Undefined operator and registration mechanics.** The bill does not identify whether the operator is the owner, charterer, manager, or another party, or allocate duties when those roles overlap. It also lacks registration deadlines, update requirements, and deregistration procedures.

32. **Section 4(b)—Incomplete reporting requirements.** “Quarterly” reports have no specified due dates, reporting periods, mandatory data fields, or certification standard. Requiring only a description of recovery activities may not produce the tonnage, depth, and timing data needed to enforce section 3.

33. **Sections 4 and 5—No express registry penalties.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. Other law might supply remedies, but this bill creates no express penalty for those failures.

34. **Sections 2, 4, and 5—Missing implementation and enforcement assignments.** Beyond NOAA’s registry role, the bill does not expressly identify an enforcement agency or provide inspection, recordkeeping, investigation, or implementing-rule procedures. Existing authority might fill some gaps, but the text does not establish how.

35. **Section 5(a)—Unclear penalty unit.** The text does not resolve whether the $1 million daily cap applies per person, vessel, operation, or separately chargeable violation. It also supplies no penalty-assessment criteria or administrative adjudication procedure.

36. **Section 5(b)—Criminal notice and willfulness.** “Willfully” is not defined, and criminal liability depends on a prohibition incorporating ambiguous thresholds and discretionary risk determinations. The government’s required proof and defendants’ fair-notice arguments would therefore be important, though ambiguity does not automatically invalidate the provision.

37. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Conflicting commencement language.** Civil penalties cover violations occurring “on or after” enactment, while the Act takes effect 180 days later. A strong harmonizing reading is that no violation exists before effectiveness, but the unnecessary mismatch invites dispute.

### International agreement, duration, and effective date

38. **Section 6—Uncertain negotiating deadline and deliverable.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly require negotiations to begin, conclude, or produce an agreement by that date. There are no specified counterparties, reporting duties, or consequences for failure.

39. **Section 6—Unclear equivalence and domestic effect.** “Prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3” does not specify whether an agreement must reproduce the exceptions, definitions, or enforcement arrangements. Negotiating an agreement does not itself expand this bill’s domestic prohibition or make foreign parties subject to it.

40. **Section 7(a)—No mechanism to obtain the Academies report.** The bill neither commissions nor funds the report and sets no deadline, required contents, or submission process. The contemplated early termination pathway therefore depends on a report the Act does not ensure will exist.

41. **Section 7(a)—Undefined termination standard and procedure.** “Without serious harm” identifies neither the relevant harms nor the acceptable evidentiary standard. “Acting on a report” also leaves unclear whether Congress must consider a particular report; a legally operative joint resolution ordinarily still requires presidential approval or a veto override.

42. **Sections 7(a)–(b)—Indefinite-duration language versus sunset.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition remains until the congressional finding, while section 7(b) ends the entire Act after ten years regardless. The provisions can likely be harmonized as alternative termination routes, but the text should expressly state that relationship.

43. **Sections 7(b) and 8—Less than ten years of operative prohibition.** The sunset runs from enactment, not the effective date. The prohibition therefore operates for approximately nine and a half years unless ended earlier.

44. **Section 7—Different consequences of early termination and sunset.** An early congressional finding ends the section 3 prohibition but does not expressly end registry duties; the ten-year sunset ends the entire Act. The text provides no transition rules for those differing outcomes.

45. **Section 7(b)—No express savings provision.** The sunset does not specify treatment of accrued penalties, pending proceedings, or outstanding reports. General federal savings law may preserve accrued liabilities, so expiration should not be assumed to erase prior violations.

46. **Section 8—Implementation window.** On the ordinary reading, this Act imposes no operative prohibition during the first 180 days after enactment. Operations in that interval remain subject to existing law, and the bill supplies no special transition rules for activity spanning the effective date.
